                                        PROJECT NO. 58482

LARGE LOAD DEMAND                                §       PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION OF
MANAGEMENT SERVICE                               §                 TEXAS
                                                 §

                         - CONFIDENTIAL DRAFT -
         ENGIE NORTH AMERICA COMMENTS ON PROPOSAL FOR PUBLICATION

          ENGIE North America Inc. (“ENGIE”) respectfully submits these comments in response
to the Public Utility Commission of Texas (“Commission”) July 30, 2026 Proposal for
Publication of new 16 TAC §25.521 relating to Large Load Demand Service, implementing Public
Utility Regulatory Act (“PURA”) §39.170 as enacted by Senate Bill 6 during the Texas 89th
Legislative Session, regarding curtailment of transmission-voltage customers during firm load
shed events – and competitive procurement of demand reductions from large load customers.

    I.       INTRODUCTION
     ENGIE appreciates the opportunity to submit these comments to the Public Utility Commission of
Texas ("Commission") regarding the proposed Large Load Demand Management Service ("LLDMS") in
Project No. 58482. ENGIE is actively evaluating large-load and behind-the-meter battery storage
opportunities in ERCOT and therefore has a direct and immediate interest in the workability of LLDMS
eligibility, metering, participation, and compensation requirements.

     ENGIE supports the Commission's objective of creating a voluntary reliability service that can provide
dependable demand reduction from large loads during qualifying emergency conditions. ENGIE
respectfully requests targeted changes and clarifications to ensure that LLDMS is technology-neutral,
measurable, and commercially workable. In particular, the final rule should recognize verified demand
reductions delivered by behind-the-meter battery storage at the point of interconnection; allow separately
measured load and uncommitted battery capacity to participate in other ERCOT services without double
counting; clarify registration, metering, Wholesale Storage Load ("WSL"), and charging treatment; and
provide compensation sufficient to attract meaningful participation.

     ENGIE notes that the Data Center Coalition ("DCC"), Texas Industrial Energy Consumers ("TIEC"),
Texas Advanced Energy Business Alliance ("TAEBA"), Voltus, Inc. ("Voltus"), Enchanted Rock, LLC
("Enchanted Rock"), and Eolian, L.P. ("Eolian") have filed comments addressing the design of LLDMS.
ENGIE shares the broader stakeholder interest in a workable and commercially viable service. These
comments add to that record by focusing on the metering, registration, revenue-stacking, and economic
considerations applicable to battery-supported participation. ENGIE does not incorporate any stakeholder


                                                     1
 filing in full and addresses only the positions expressly stated in these comments.

II. COMMENTS
        A. The final rule should expressly permit a large load to use behind-the-meter battery
storage to satisfy its LLDMS obligation.

     The final rule should measure performance based on the verified reduction in net demand at the
applicable point of interconnection or settlement meter. If a non-exporting behind-the-meter battery
discharges during an LLDMS deployment and produces the required reduction in the large load's net
ERCOT demand, that reduction should qualify even if the underlying end-use equipment does not reduce
consumption by the same amount.

     The reliability benefit arises from the reduction in the participant’s withdrawal from the ERCOT
system, not necessarily from a corresponding reduction in the customer’s internal energy consumption. For
example, if a participant withdraws 100 MW before an LLDMS deployment and reduces its net withdrawal
to 50 MW during the deployment, ERCOT receives a 50 MW reliability benefit. Whether that reduction
results from curtailment of the underlying load or discharge from onsite battery storage should not affect
eligibility, provided the reduction is measurable and verifiable at the applicable point of interconnection or
settlement meter.

     The large load would remain the LLDMS participant and contractual counterparty, with the battery
serving as an enabling resource. This performance-based approach would allow each participant to select
the operational solution best suited to its facility while preserving ERCOT's ability to verify the delivered
megawatts and enforce the participant's obligation.

     Technology neutrality will broaden participation. Large loads have different operating profiles and
may be unable to interrupt core operations without significant reliability, safety, or commercial
consequences. Storage can provide a measurable reduction in grid demand without requiring an equivalent
reduction in the underlying end-use load. The final rule should not exclude this technically capable
response.

The Commission should coordinate LLDMS with the minimum billing demand framework in
Project No. 58000.

       The interaction between the two rulemakings could create conflicting regulatory signals. Under
Project No. 58482, large loads are encouraged to reduce withdrawals from the ERCOT system during
qualifying reliability events. At the same time, minimum billing-demand requirements adopted under
Project No. 58000 could require a participating large load to pay transmission charges based on demand
that does not reflect its verified LLDMS reduction. In that circumstance, ERCOT would receive the



                                                      2
 reliability benefit of the customer’s response, while the customer could lose part of the economic value
associated with reducing its demand.

         This disconnect could weaken incentives for large loads to participate in LLDMS. ENGIE therefore
requests that the Commission coordinate the two rulemakings and clarify how verified LLDMS
performance will be treated in determining applicable transmission billing demand, including Net
Coincident Peak (“NCP”) and (potentially) 12 Coincident Peak (“12CP”) demand. The final frameworks
should avoid penalizing a large load for providing a demand reduction that ERCOT has requested and
verified for reliability purposes.
       B. ERCOT has developed a “Netted Network” concept enhancing existing market
configurations governed by existing ERCOT protocols that further augments the Private Use
Network framework and allows participation by distinct, measurable portions of a site.
     The proposed eligibility restrictions may be read to disqualify an entire large-load site if any portion
of the site participates in another reliability or ancillary service. ENGIE requests that the Commission
clarify that the eligibility restrictions in proposed §25.521(c)(2) are intended to prevent double counting of
the same committed megawatts, rather than prohibit participation by an entire site or facility capable of
providing multiple, distinct, and independently measurable services. Accordingly, the prohibition against
dual participation should apply only to capacity committed to another reliability, demand-response, or
market obligation during an overlapping LLDMS commitment period, and not to an entire site, facility, or
asset.

     ENGIE requests the Commission’s support in furthering the “Netted Network” concept ERCOT is
developing that would: enhance ERCOT’s visibility and control of additional resources, bring vital voltage
and reactive power support to the reliability of the grid, and incentivize investment in additional resources.
ENGIE recommends that the Commission direct ERCOT to develop clear metering and accounting
requirements that provide for: (1) settlement-quality measurement of the large load’s withdrawals; (2)
separate accounting of the megawatts committed to the LLDMS obligation; (3) settlement-quality
measurement of battery injection; and (4) separate accounting of battery capacity participating in the energy
market, ancillary services, or other authorized programs.

     The final rule should expressly permit participation by separately measurable portions of a large-load
facility or behind-the-meter battery, provided ERCOT can verify through appropriate metering, telemetry,
and settlement controls that the same megawatts are not committed to multiple obligations simultaneously.
For example, if a 100 MW battery reserves 40 MW for LLDMS, ERCOT should permit the remaining 60
MW to participate in other authorized markets or programs, provided telemetry and settlements verify
distinct capacity reservations. Likewise, a large-load campus should be permitted to designate a separately
measurable portion of its demand-response capability for LLDMS while another independently measurable


                                                      3
 portion participates in a different eligible service.

     This capacity- and time-specific approach would prevent double counting while maximizing the
amount of flexible load and storage capability available to ERCOT. ENGIE therefore recommends that the
final rule expressly provide that eligibility restrictions apply only to overlapping committed capacity and
not to entire sites, facilities, or assets capable of demonstrating separate and verifiable performance.

        C. The Commission should clarify the treatment of onsite storage under net-metering,
registration, Wholesale Storage Load (WSL), and retail charging rules.
     The final rule should clarify whether the net-metering exclusion applies to the customer, the entire site,
a particular meter, or only the specific arrangement subject to a curtailment obligation. Without this clarity,
a large load cannot determine with confidence whether adding a non-exporting battery, using separate
meters, or operating within a Private Use Network (“PUN”) would affect LLDMS eligibility.

     The Commission should direct ERCOT to clarify how a behind-the-meter battery supporting LLDMS
must be registered and how its charging energy will be classified. Specifically, the final rule or
implementing requirements should state whether storage supporting an LLDMS obligation may qualify for
WSL treatment and, if so, under what circumstances. The framework should also expressly distinguish
when charging energy will be treated as wholesale charging and when it will be treated as retail
consumption.

        The Commission should further clarify that existing unused import capability may be used to
charge a behind-the-meter battery during normal operations without jeopardizing the large load’s LLDMS
eligibility, provided the charging arrangement complies with applicable interconnection, metering,
registration, and settlement requirements. These clarifications are necessary for prospective participants to
evaluate the costs and operational feasibility of battery-supported LLDMS participation.

     D. LLDMS may support transmission emergencies if deployment conditions are clearly defined.

     ENGIE supports making LLDMS available to address qualifying transmission emergencies, provided
the final rule establishes clear and transparent deployment parameters. ERCOT should define in advance
the geographic areas in which participants may be deployed, the system conditions and criteria that may
trigger deployment, and any applicable limits on deployment duration.

     Compensation for a transmission-related deployment should remain consistent with the compensation
otherwise applicable to an LLDMS deployment. Participants should not face reduced or uncertain
compensation based solely on the type or location of the reliability condition that caused ERCOT to deploy
the service. The rules should also protect participants from open-ended deployment obligations by
prescribing defined duration limits or other reasonable operational boundaries.



                                                        4
      These requirements would allow transmission-related deployment to provide additional reliability
value while giving prospective participants sufficient clarity regarding where, when, and for how long their
committed capacity may be called.

       E. The payment structure and participation rules should support sufficient reliability-
resource participation.
     LLDMS is proposed as an as-needed service associated with elevated emergency risk, with
deployment during qualifying EEA conditions. The limited and uncertain number of deployment hours
materially constrains the revenue available to support dedicated storage investment. ENGIE prepared the
following illustrative revenue assessment to show the potential magnitude of LLDMS revenue under an
assumed clearing price at the proposed offer cap.

Illustrative 100 MW BESS LLDMS Revenue Assessment
Assumption / Result                                 Value                 Explanation
Battery capacity                                    100 MW                Illustrative dedicated BESS
Clearing price                                      $5,000/MWh            Proposed offer cap
                                                                          Limited annual deployment
Deployed hours                                      4 hours/year          assumption because dispatch is tied
                                                                          to qualifying EEA conditions
Deployment revenue                                  $2.0 million/year     $1.67/kW-month
Called but not deployed                             2 hours/year          Illustrative availability assumption
Availability payment                                25% of clearing price $0.25 million/year
Total illustrative revenue                          $2.25 million/year    $1.88/kW-month
     This analysis is illustrative and is not a forecast of clearing prices, procurement frequency,
     deployment duration, or actual project economics. It assumes no reduction from the proposed
     $54 million annual program budget and excludes other battery revenues, charging costs, losses,
     operating costs, degradation, capital costs, and financing costs.
     ENGIE recognizes that LLDMS is not intended to finance the full cost of behind-the-meter battery
storage on a standalone basis. However, the program should not be designed in a manner that effectively
excludes battery-supported participation. Even at the proposed $5,000/MWh offer cap, the illustrative
LLDMS revenue appears insufficient, on a standalone basis, to support investment in a dedicated 100 MW
BESS without access to other revenue streams. The $54 million annual budget could further constrain
revenues as participation grows or if procurement quantities or payments must be reduced to remain within
the cap. Accordingly, the final rule should preserve access to other revenue streams for battery capacity and
time periods not committed to LLDMS, subject to safeguards against overlapping obligations.

1.       Revenue stacking increases the availability of reliability resources.
The final rule should permit battery capacity and time periods not committed to LLDMS to participate in
other authorized ERCOT services, subject to safeguards against overlapping commitments. Without access
to additional revenue streams, fewer battery projects may be financially viable and fewer large loads may
be able to offer battery-supported demand reduction through LLDMS. Battery Storage resources have been



                                                      5
 identified as solutions for operational reliability, such as Voltage Ride Through requirements. By allowing
uncommitted capacity to earn other revenues can support additional investment and participation, thereby
increasing the quantity of flexible resources available to ERCOT during emergency conditions. This
approach would preserve the contracted LLDMS capability while ensuring that the same capacity is not
committed to multiple obligations simultaneously.

Allowing uncommitted capacity to earn revenue from other authorized ERCOT services may also reduce
pressure to increase the LLDMS program budget by supporting participation without shifting the full cost
of battery economics to retail electric providers and customers.

2.       The program budget should balance reliability needs with forward cost certainty.

     ENGIE recognizes that a defined program budget provides important forward cost certainty for retail
electric providers and other market participants responsible for managing program costs. The Commission
should therefore avoid an open-ended or automatically adjusting budget that could expose retailers and
customers to uncertain or unexpectedly large costs.

     Before finalizing the program budget, the Commission should evaluate expected procurement
quantities, clearing prices, availability periods, and deployment scenarios to determine whether the
proposed budget can attract sufficient participation within a predictable cost framework. Once established,
the budget should operate as a transparent cap for the applicable program period.

     If experience demonstrates that the budget materially limits ERCOT’s ability to procure the reliability
quantity authorized by the Commission, any proposed adjustment should apply prospectively and occur
through a transparent Commission review with advance notice, stakeholder input, and consideration of the
resulting costs to retail electric providers and customers. The framework should not permit automatic,
retroactive, or unlimited increases in program costs.

3.       The availability payment should support readiness within the established program budget.

     The proposed 25 percent payment for awarded capacity that is available but not deployed provides
value for maintaining readiness, reserving capacity, managing state of charge, and limiting other market
activity. The Commission should evaluate whether the availability payment is sufficient to attract reliable
participation while remaining within the established program budget and providing predictable program
costs. Any future change to the availability-payment percentage should apply prospectively and be subject
to the same transparent review applicable to other material program-cost changes.




                                                        6
         F. Requested Relief
ENGIE respectfully requests that the Commission revise or clarify the final rule to:

    •   permit a large load to use behind-the-meter battery storage to satisfy an LLDMS obligation when
        the required reduction is verified at the applicable point of interconnection or settlement meter;
    •   direct ERCOT to develop separate or net-net metering, telemetry, baseline, and settlement
        requirements that prevent double counting while allowing distinct, measurable portions of a site
        and uncommitted battery capacity to participate in other services;
    •   clarify the scope of the net-metering exclusion and the treatment of PUNs and battery registration,
        including whether storage supporting LLDMS may qualify for WSL treatment, when battery
        charging will be classified as wholesale or retail consumption, and whether existing unused import
        capability may be used for charging without jeopardizing LLDMS eligibility;
            o   expeditious support for the Netted Networks concept that ERCOT presented during the
                August 21, 2026 Large Load Working Group meeting with stakeholders;
    •   permit LLDMS deployment during qualifying transmission emergencies only under clearly defined
        geographic and operational criteria, with transparent deployment triggers, consistent compensation,
        and reasonable limits on deployment duration;
    •   establish a defined and transparent program budget that provides forward cost certainty; evaluate
        whether the proposed budget and availability payment can attract sufficient reliability participation
        within that cost framework; and require that any material adjustment be prospective and subject to
        advance notice, stakeholder input, and consideration of impacts on retail electric providers and
        customers;
    •   allow capacity and time periods not committed to LLDMS to participate in other authorized
        ERCOT services, subject to safeguards against overlapping obligations, so that the program does
        not unnecessarily limit investment, participation, or the quantity of flexible reliability resources
        available to ERCOT; and
    •   coordinate Project Nos. 58482 and 58000 and clarify the treatment of verified LLDMS performance
        in determining applicable transmission billing demand, including NCP and 12CP demand, so that
        minimum billing-demand requirements do not create conflicting regulatory signals or weaken
        incentives to provide requested reliability reductions.




                                                     7
 III. CONCLUSION
    ENGIE appreciates the opportunity to submit these comments and respectfully urges the Commission
to adopt a performance-based, technology-neutral LLDMS framework that preserves reliability, prevents
double counting, and provides sufficient flexibility and economic value to attract meaningful participation
from large loads and onsite storage.



                                                   Respectfully submitted,

                                                   /s/ Lindsey Hughes

other authorized ERCOT services, subject to safeguards against overlapping commitments. Without access
to additional revenue streams, fewer battery projects may be financially viable and fewer large loads may
be able to offer battery-supported demand reduction through LLDMS. Battery Storage resources have been




                                                      5
 identified as solutions for operational reliability, such as Voltage Ride Through requirements. By allowing
uncommitted capacity to earn other revenues call support additional investment and participation, thereby
increasing the quantity of flexible resources available to ERCOT during emergency conditions. This
approach would preserve the contracted LLDMS capability while ensuring that the same capacity is not
committed to multiple obligations simultaneously.

Allowing uncommitted capacity to earn revenue from other authorized ERCOT services may also reduce
pressure to increase the LLDMS program budget by supporting participation without shifting the full cost
of battery economics to retail electric providers and customers.

2.       The program budget should balance reliability needs with forward cost certainty.

     ENGIE recognizes that a defined program budget provides important forward cost certainty for retail
electric providers and other market participants responsible for managing program costs. The Commission
should therefore avoid an open-ended or automatically adjusting budget that could expose retailers and
customers to uncertain or unexpectedly large costs.

     Before finalizing the program budget, the Commission should evaluate expected procurement
quantities, clearing prices, availability periods, and deployment scenarios to determine whether the
proposed budget can attract sufficient participation within a predictable cost framework. Once established,
the budget should operate as a transparent cap for the applicable program period.

     If experience demonstrates that the budget materially limits ERCOT's ability to procure the reliability
quantity authorized by the Commission, any proposed adjustment should apply prospectively and occur
through a transparent Commission review with advance notice, stakeholder input, and consideration ofthe
resulting costs to retail electric providers and customers. The framework should not permit automatic,
retroactive, or unlimited increases in program costs.

3.       The availability payment should support readiness within the established program budget.

     The proposed 25 percent payment for awarded capacity that is available but not deployed provides
value for maintaining readiness, reserving capacity, managing state of charge, and limiting other market
activity. The Commission should evaluate whether the availability payment is sufficient to attract reliable
participation while remaining within the established program budget and providing predictable program
costs. Any future change to the availability-payment percentage should apply prospectively and be subject
to the same transparent review applicable to other material program-cost changes.

         F. Requested Relief
ENGIE respectfully requests that the Commission revise or clarify the final rule to:

    •   permit a large load to use behind-the-meter battery storage to satisfy an LLDMS obligation when
        the required reduction is verified at the applicable point of interconnection or settlement meter;
    •   direct ERCOT to develop separate or net-net metering, telemetry, baseline, and settlement
        requirements that prevent double counting while allowing distinct, measurable portions of a site
        and uncommitted battery capacity to participate in other services;
    •   clarify the scope ofthe net-metering exclusion and the treatment of PUNs and battery registration,
        including whether storage supporting LLDMS may qualify for WSL treatment, when battery
        charging will be classified as wholesale or retail consumption, and whether existing unused import
        capability may be used for charging without jeopardizing LLDMS eligibility;
            o   expeditious support for the Netted Networks concept that ERCOT presented during the
                August 21, 2026 Large Load Working Group meeting with stakeholders;
    •   permit LLDMS deployment during qualifying transmission emergencies only under clearly defined
        geographic and operational criteria, with transparent deployment triggers, consistent compensation,
        and reasonable limits on deployment duration;
    •   establish a defined and transparent program budget that provides forward cost certainty; evaluate
        whether the proposed budget and availability payment can attract sufficient reliability participation
        within that cost framework; and require that any material adjustment be prospective and subject to
        advance notice, stakeholder input, and consideration of impacts on retail electric providers and
        customers;
    •   allow capacity and time periods not committed to LLDMS to participate in other authorized
        ERCOT services, subject to safeguards against overlapping obligations, so that the program does
        not unnecessarily limit investment, participation, or the quantity of flexible reliability resources
        available to ERCOT; and
    •   coordinate Project Nos. 58482 and 58000 and clarify the treatment ofverified LLDMS performance
        in determining applicable transmission billing demand, including NCP and 12CP demand, so that
        minimum billing-demand requirements do not create conflicting regulatory signals or weaken
        incentives to provide requested reliability reductions.
